extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (examining subject matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. 101)
extracted.subtask_description: A step-by-step USPTO worksheet for examining patent claims under 35 U.S.C. §101, including determining what applicant invented, whether the claim is in a statutory category, whether it is directed to an abstract idea, and whether additional elements amount to 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify what applicant invented
rubrics_metrics.description: Review the disclosure to identify what applicant considers as the invention. This can be a brief description and should not merely reproduce the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on the takeaway of what the invention is directed to (e.g., 'a way to improve the functioning of the GPS system'). Use MPEP 2103(I) as authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) of the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Construe the claim in accordance with its broadest reasonable interpretation for the purposes of the eligibility analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the BRI when identifying whether the claim recites an abstract idea and when determining the scope of additional elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory category check (Step 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claimed invention falls within one of the four statutory categories of invention (process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter). Choose A (Yes) or B (No).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim could be amended to fall within a statutory category, it is recommended to continue the SME analysis under that assumption; make that assumption clear in the record and consider suggesting an amendment to the applicant. If no amendment is possible, conclude SME analysis and proceed to other patentability requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea (Step 2A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide if the claim recites a concept similar to those courts have found to be abstract (e.g., fundamental economic practices, certain methods of organizing human activity, ideas themselves, mathematical relationships/formulae). Choose A (No), B (Yes, streamlined), or C (Yes, full explanation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If (C) identify the limitation(s) in the claim that recite the abstract idea and explain why the recited subject matter is an abstract idea. Assistance can be obtained from the case law chart and the 2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify claim limitations that recite the abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify the particular claim limitation(s) that set forth or describe the abstract idea (e.g., limitations that recite mathematical operations such as 'estimate,' 'calculate,' 'create').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why the identified limitation(s) are considered an abstract idea (for example, courts have treated mathematical operations and organizing/manipulating information as judicial exceptions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Are there additional elements beyond the abstract idea? (Step 2B - A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim recites any elements (features/limitations/steps) beyond the abstract idea. Choose (1) No or (2) Yes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If No (no other elements), conclude SME analysis by making a §101 rejection and continue with examination under other patentability requirements (use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015). If Yes, list the additional elements and continue the analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate significance of additional elements (search for an 'inventive concept')
rubrics_metrics.description: The additional elements must show an 'inventive concept' — evaluate all identified additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not important how the elements are characterized or how many considerations apply from the list — what matters is the significance of the additional elements relative to the applicant's invention. Consider the applicant's invention (Section I) when evaluating significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improves another technology or technical field
rubrics_metrics.description: One possible indicator that additional elements provide significantly more is that they 'improve another technology or technical field.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate how the claimed elements produce a technological improvement beyond the abstract idea (examples in worksheet show improvements to digital image processing or GPS signal acquisition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improves the functioning of a computer itself
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional elements may be significant if they improve the functioning of the computer itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show that the limitations change how the computer operates (not merely use a computer to perform the abstract idea in a generic way).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applies the abstract idea with, or by use of, a particular machine
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying the abstract idea using a particular machine can support a finding of significantly more (but the machine must not be just a generic computer performing generic functions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on merely appending generic computer components or adding phrases like 'apply it' or instructions to implement the idea on a computer. Show specific machine implementation or concerted action among recited components (example: server + mobile device interaction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing
rubrics_metrics.description: An element that effects a transformation of a particular article to a different state or thing supports eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify how the claim's steps transform or change a physical or tangible article or data representation in a meaningful way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adds a specific limitation beyond well‑understood, routine, and conventional activity
rubrics_metrics.description: An additional element that adds a specific limitation other than what is well‑understood, routine, and conventional in the field can provide significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid merely appending known industry activities at a high level of generality; show that the claim adds a novel and concrete limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adds unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular, useful application can weigh in favor of eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on insignificant extrasolution activity (e.g., mere data gathering). The steps must meaningfully limit the claim to a particular practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adds meaningful limitations beyond merely linking to a technological environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional elements that add meaningful limitations — more than generally linking the abstract idea to a particular technological environment — support a finding of significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show how the limitations meaningfully limit the scope of the abstract idea, not merely tie it to a device or setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic computer components do not alone decide eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Generic computer components in a claim (e.g., 'processor,' 'memory') alone do not by themselves confer or preclude eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how the generic components function in combination with other claim elements to determine whether they amount to significantly more than the abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined analysis when eligibility is self‑evident
rubrics_metrics.description: If eligibility is self-evident, a streamlined analysis may be appropriate and a full eligibility analysis is not needed (choose option B in Step 2A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to training materials (e.g., February 2015 Training Slides) for examples of when a streamlined analysis is appropriate; conclude SME analysis and proceed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office action drafting and use of form paragraphs for §101 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim is directed to a judicial exception without significantly more, make a §101 rejection and use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015 in Custom OACs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sample rejection wording is provided in the worksheet and should be used in the Office action. If elements could be added to render a claim eligible, identify them and consider suggesting amendments to the applicant in the Office action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclude SME analysis and continue examination under other patentability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim is eligible (i.e., amounts to significantly more) conclude the SME analysis and continue examination under each of the other patentability requirements; if not, make a §101 rejection and continue with examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If needed, clarify the record with remarks explaining why the claim is or is not eligible (e.g., 'the claim recites the abstract idea of X, but amounts to significantly more with additional element Y because ABC').

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider suggesting claim amendments to applicant
rubrics_metrics.description: If no additional elements are present that would render the claim eligible, identify elements in the disclosure that could be added to the claim to potentially make it eligible and consider suggesting them to the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide specific candidate elements from the disclosure in the Office action for applicant consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate additional elements individually and in combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider all identified additional elements both individually and in combination to determine whether the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many considerations overlap; more than one may apply. The analysis should assess the combined effect of limitations on the claim's scope and practical application.
